sections.learningObjectives:
- Distinguish between Excludes1 and Excludes2 notes and explain when two conditions may or may not be reported together.
- Apply Includes notes to determine which terms and conditions are classifiable to a given ICD-10-CM code.
- Interpret code-first and use-additional-code notes to sequence underlying etiology and manifestation codes correctly.
- Recognize how ICD-10-CM instructional notes guide accurate, complete, and non-conflicting code assignment.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

An Excludes1 note is like a sign that says two flavors can never be mixed into the same dish — they are so different that you can only choose one.

### Question 2

An Excludes2 note is like a sign that says a topping is not included with your meal, but you are still allowed to order it as an extra — you can have both.

### Question 3

An Includes note is like the label on a box that lists everything you are allowed to put inside it — it tells you what fits.

### Question 4

A code-first note is like a recipe that says the base ingredient must go in the bowl before the flavoring — the underlying cause is the base that goes first.

### Question 5

A use-additional-code note is like a reminder that a story is missing an important detail, so you should add that detail to make the whole picture clear.

### Question 6

An Excludes1 note is like a rule that two teams can never play on the same field at once — no matter what the paperwork says, you cannot put them together.

### Question 7

An Excludes2 note is like saying fries are not included with the burger, but you can still order fries — you list both items on the bill.

### Question 8

An Excludes1 note is like saying a light switch is either ON or OFF — it cannot be both at the same moment.

### Question 9

An Includes note says "these things go in this box," while an Excludes1 note says "these things can never go in this box."

### Question 10

Excludes1 is a hard "never together" rule, and Excludes2 is a softer "not part of this, but you can still add it" rule.

### Question 11

If the label on a bin lists "crayons," then crayons belong in that bin — an Includes note works the same way for a diagnosis code.

### Question 12

If the label says "soda (pop)," then both "soda" and "pop" belong in the same bin — the note is just giving you both names.

### Question 13

An Includes note is like a menu that shows "popular choices" — it shows examples, but that does not mean nothing else fits.

### Question 14

A code-first note says the cause goes before the effect — like listing the rain before the puddle it made.

### Question 15

A use-additional-code note is like saying "be sure to write down what color and size it is, too," so the description is complete.

### Question 16

One note says "put the cause first," and the matching note says "don't forget the effect" — together they make one complete pair.

### Question 17

The cause is the main character that enters the story first, and the effect is the second character that follows.

### Question 18

The manifestation is the effect, and the effect cannot lead the parade — the cause always marches in front.

### Question 19

Think of diabetes as the root of a plant and the complication as a leaf — the root is written down first, then the leaf.

### Question 20

The Tabular List is like the main rule book where the important instructions are printed next to each code.

### Question 21

A note at the top of a page applies to everything listed on that page — the category note works the same way for all its subcodes.

### Question 22

If two things can never be true at the same time, you figure out which one is actually true and record only that one — and ask for help if the notes are confusing.

### Question 23

An Excludes2 note says two things are separate items, not one item, but you can still own both at once.

### Question 24

If the patient truly has both, you write both on the list — Excludes2 gives you permission to do exactly that.

### Question 25

A condition you are born with and a condition you develop later are like two different keys that cannot open the same lock at once.

### Question 26

These notes are like guardrails on a road — they keep the coding on the right path so nothing is missed or doubled up.

### Question 27

Clean, correct codes are like correct answers on a big national survey — if everyone follows the rules, the results can be trusted.

### Question 28

The word "with" in an Includes note is like a two-for-one deal — the main item and its add-on are both covered by one ticket.

### Question 29

"Excludes1" is a special label that means "these two things can never be true at the same time."

### Question 30

Excludes2 says "this item is not in this box — it lives in another box, but you can carry both boxes at once."

### Question 31

An Excludes1 note is a firm "these two can never share the same bill" rule.

### Question 32

A broken bone from an accident and a broken bone from a disease are two different stories — you can only tell one of them with the code.

### Question 33

If both are real and both happened, both get written down — Excludes2 is the rule that makes that okay.

### Question 34

Excludes2 says "two things can live side by side," while Excludes1 says "two things can never live in the same place."

### Question 35

The cause is the driver, so it goes in the front seat; the effect rides in the back.

### Question 36

The note is like asking "which exact germ is it?" and reminding you to write that answer down too.

### Question 37

The note says "don't stop yet — there is one more important detail to add."

### Question 38

The note is stuck on the effect and points backward, saying "make sure the cause comes before me."

### Question 39

Even if the effect is what brought the patient in, the rule says the cause must be written first.

### Question 40

If your name is on the guest list, you are definitely allowed inside — the Includes note is the guest list.

### Question 41

Includes says "these go in," and Excludes2 says "these stay out but can stand beside it."

### Question 42

When two things can't both be true, find out which one is true and write that one down — and ask the doctor if the chart is unclear.

### Question 43

Following the rules means fewer "returned mail" claims, so the office gets paid smoothly and correctly.

### Question 44

Excludes1 pairs up things that are opposites that cannot both be true at once.

### Question 45

Excludes2 pairs up two separate things that can comfortably exist at the same time.

### Question 46

The note says "not in this box, but you can still carry both boxes" — that is the Excludes2 rule.

### Question 47

These notes are real rules, not friendly suggestions — like a stop sign rather than a wave.

### Question 48

When you are not sure about an important rule, the smart move is to ask the person whose job is to know the rule.

### Question 49

An Includes note is like a definition that gives examples so you know exactly what fits under the code.

### Question 50

You read the label on the box first: one label says "never together," the other says "together is fine."

### Question 51

Excludes2 is not a red flag — it is just a label saying "these are two different things, and that is okay."

### Question 52

Putting the effect before the cause is like saying the egg came before the chicken — the rule says the cause goes first.

### Question 53

The note tells you what kind of detail is missing, and the chart tells you the exact detail — put them together to pick the right code.

### Question 54

The principal diagnosis is the headline of the story, and the rules say the cause must be the headline when a code-first note applies.

### Question 55

If two things can't both be true, report only the one that is true and leave the other off the bill.

### Question 56

The list is a "for example" list, not a "these and only these" list — a matching condition can still fit.

### Question 57

One note says "cause first," and its partner says "then add the effect" — together they spell out the full, correct order.

### Question 58

The instructions are printed right next to the code they belong to, like a sticky note on the exact page it applies to.

### Question 59

Skin and nails are different items — each gets its own line on the bill, and Excludes2 says that is allowed.

### Question 60

When your word is on the approved list, you are cleared to use that code — no extra phone call needed.

### Question 61

This record has two rules at once: put the cause first and add the effect, but leave out the item that can never share the bill with the cause.

### Question 62

Being told a book cannot sit on a certain shelf does not mean the book doesn't exist — it just goes on its own shelf.

### Question 63

The note says "put the cause before me" — the cause always goes first.

### Question 64

The note says "there's more to this story — write down the extra detail, too."

### Question 65

The note draws a hard line: the listed conditions and these codes can never be on the same bill.

### Question 66

The note says "these aren't in this box, but you can carry this box and that one at the same time."

### Question 67

If every puzzle piece is placed correctly, the finished picture is trustworthy — accurate codes make the practice's data trustworthy.

### Question 68

If the label already explains what the short word means, you can confidently put it in the right box.

### Question 69

A rule posted at the top of a section covers everything in that section, not just the first line.

### Question 70

The note literally tells you to "add another code," like a reminder to write down one more detail.

### Question 71

One pair of items is allowed together, and the other pair is not — follow each rule for its own pair.

### Question 72

The note says "not in the box, but you can have both" — that is exactly what Excludes2 means.

### Question 73

If the rule says the cause must be listed but the chart forgot to name the cause, you ask the doctor what it is.

### Question 74

Excludes1 is a hard "no together," and Excludes2 is a soft "not part of this, but together is okay."

### Question 75

Only apply the rule for the item you actually have — a rule about apples doesn't matter when you're holding an orange.

### Question 76

One cause can have several effects — the cause still goes first, and all the effects line up after it.

### Question 77

Even if the chart lists both, the rule says they can't share a bill — find out which one is real.

### Question 78

Excludes2 gives the green light to list both — they are separate but both true.

### Question 79

Code-first is a firm rule, not a suggestion — the cause must always go first.

### Question 80

The note says "write down the main problem AND the body part it affects" — both go on the list.

### Question 81

Sending in a bill with two things that can't both be true is like turning in homework with a wrong answer — it gets marked wrong.

### Question 82

An Includes note is the "what's inside this box" list that helps you match the right item to the right box.

### Question 83

Excludes2 is not a "never together" rule — it is a "not part of the same code, but can happen at once" rule.

### Question 84

Before you act, read the sign: is it a "never together" sign or a "together is fine" sign?

### Question 85

When the rule book has a note, read it and follow it — that's the whole game.
